candidate_sources.title: Fact sheet - Rice bacterial leaf blight (418) - Lucid Apps (Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds)
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms vary by stage: seedlings show grey-green streaks from tips and margins that join, turn yellowish-white with wavy edges, and wilt (kresek); older plants show pale yellow streaks with wavy margins. Milky bacterial ooze dries as a crust. Caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae; bacteria enter through natural openings and wounds, move in the xylem, and spread in irrigation/floodwater and wind-driven rain.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial blight - IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: IRRI Rice Doctor fact sheet on bacterial blight of rice caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae, covering water-soaked lesions, wilting (kresek) of seedlings, yellow to white lesions with wavy margins, bacterial ooze, favorable conditions, and management including resistant varieties and field sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Rice bacterial blight | Plant Disease, Description, Symptoms, & Control | Britannica
candidate_sources.snippet: Rice bacterial blight, a deadly disease caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae. Describes wilting and yellowing of leaves (kresek), pale-yellow to white wavy-margined lesions, bacterial ooze, disease cycle, and control through resistant cultivars and sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Bacterial Leaf Blight Disease of Rice Caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae in Madagascar | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: APS Plant Disease note reporting bacterial leaf blight of rice caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae, with diagnostic symptom description and pathogen identification/confirmation.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial leaf streak of rice
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet on bacterial leaf streak of rice caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola. Symptoms are narrow, dark-greenish, water-soaked, interveinal streaks of various lengths on leaf blades; lesions enlarge and turn yellow-orange to brown with amber-colored bacterial exudates. The main difference between leaf streak and leaf blight is the shape of the lesion edges: straight in leaf streak, wavy in leaf blight.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial leaf streak - IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank fact sheet describing bacterial leaf streak: water-soaked, translucent to yellow interveinal linear streaks; yellow exudates or amber droplets of bacterial ooze under humid conditions. The disease occurs in areas with high temperature and high humidity, is transmitted through seeds and infected stubbles, and is managed with chemicals and resistant varieties. Yield loss of 8 to 32%.

candidate_sources.title: Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola (bacterial leaf streak of rice) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet for Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola, the causal agent of bacterial leaf streak of rice, covering identity, distribution, symptoms, biology, and management. BLS spread is limited to tropical and subtropical Asia, Northern Australia, and parts of Western Africa.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Panicle Blight of Rice in Arkansas (FSA-7580)
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension factsheet on bacterial panicle blight of rice, covering the causal pathogen Burkholderia glumae, diagnostic symptoms (sheath rot, panicle discoloration and sterility, two-toned grain with brown discoloration on the lower third to half of the grain, green panicle branches up to the infected grain), favorable conditions, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Panicle Blight | LSU AgCenter
candidate_sources.snippet: LSU AgCenter rice disease page on bacterial panicle blight caused by Burkholderia glumae. Describes symptoms including grain spotting, rot, and panicle blight that can result in yield losses of 75% or more, and provides disease management information for the southern United States.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Panicle Blight and Burkholderia glumae: From Pathogen Biology to Disease Control | Phytopathology
candidate_sources.snippet: APS Phytopathology review article covering bacterial panicle blight (BPB) caused by Burkholderia glumae and B. gladioli. Discusses pathogen biology, panicle blight symptoms (long gray lesions with red to dark brown scar edges, two-toned grain discoloration), high temperature/high humidity conditions at heading favoring outbreaks, host resistance QTLs, and biocontrol and chemical disease control strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Rice Blast Disease - UF/IFAS EDIS - University of Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: Rice blast is caused by Magnaporthe oryzae (formerly Pyricularia oryzae). Leaf lesions are diamond shaped with a gray or white center and brown or reddish-brown border, 10-15 mm long. Covers symptoms (leaf, node, neck/panicle blast), disease cycle, favorable conditions, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Rice Blast / Rice / Agriculture: Pest Management Guidelines / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines for rice blast caused by Magnaporthe oryzae. Detailed description of symptoms on leaves, nodes, and panicles, disease development, and integrated management including resistant cultivars and fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Leaf and Neck Blast of Rice FSA2211 - University of Arkansas Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension factsheet on leaf and neck blast of rice caused by Pyricularia oryzae (Magnaporthe oryzae). Describes elliptical/diamond-shaped leaf lesions, neck and node infection, conditions favoring disease, and management with resistant varieties, water management, and fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Magnaporthe oryzae (rice blast disease) - CABI Plantwise Plus Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet for Magnaporthe oryzae (rice blast disease), formerly Pyricularia oryzae/grisea. Covers identity, host range, symptoms by plant part, biology and ecology, geographic distribution, and prevention and control.

candidate_sources.title: Cochliobolus miyabeanus (brown leaf spot of rice) - CABI Compendium datasheet
candidate_sources.snippet: Cochliobolus miyabeanus (teleomorph; anamorph Bipolaris oryzae, formerly Helminthosporium oryzae) causes brown spot, a common disease of seedlings and on leaves, leaf sheaths, panicles, glumes and seeds of developing and mature rice plants. Datasheet covers Identity, Distribution, Hosts, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Seedborne Aspects, Impacts and Prevention/Control. Seedling mortality up to 60% in the Philippines; yield reduced up to 40% in India and Nigeria.

candidate_sources.title: Fact sheet - Rice brown leaf spot (427) - Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds (Lucid)
candidate_sources.snippet: Fact sheet on rice brown leaf spot caused by Cochliobolus miyabeanus (Bipolaris oryzae). Describes circular to oval lesions with light grey/brown centres and reddish-brown margins on leaves, plus infection of glumes and seeds; covers source of infection, spread, host range, and management/control recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Brown Spot of Rice: Worldwide Disease Impact, Phenotypic and Genetic Diversity of the Causal Pathogen Bipolaris oryzae, and Management of the Disease - Plant Pathology (BSPP), 2025
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review of brown spot of rice: worldwide disease impact, symptoms (small circular dark brown to purple-brown spots progressing to oval lesions with light brown/grey centres and reddish-brown margins), phenotypic and genetic diversity of the causal pathogen Bipolaris oryzae, and integrated management of the disease.

candidate_sources.title: Cochliobolus miyabeanus - Wikipedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Cochliobolus miyabeanus (anamorph Bipolaris oryzae) is the fungus causing brown spot disease of rice and was historically implicated in the 1943 Bengal famine. Article covers host, symptoms, disease cycle, environment, and management.

candidate_sources.title: What Causes Rice Leaf Smut: Treating Rice With Leaf Smut Disease | Gardening Know How
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf smut, caused by the fungus Entyloma oryzae, is a widely distributed but minor disease of rice. The fungus produces slightly raised black spots (sori) on both sides of leaves and on sheaths and stalks; heavily infected leaves turn yellow and leaf tips die and turn gray. Cleaning up debris at the end of each growing season can prevent spread; high nitrogen levels increase incidence.

candidate_sources.title: Rice | Texas Plant Disease Handbook
candidate_sources.snippet: The Texas Plant Disease Handbook entry for rice covers fungal diseases of rice including leaf smut caused by Entyloma oryzae, describing the black sori on leaves, sheaths and stalks, late-season occurrence, and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Compendium of Rice Diseases and Pests, Second Edition
candidate_sources.snippet: APS Press Compendium of Rice Diseases and Pests (Second Edition) — authoritative reference covering rice diseases including leaf smut (Entyloma oryzae) with descriptions of symptoms, the causal pathogen, disease cycle, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Rice Sheath Blight
candidate_sources.snippet: Sheath blight of rice, caused by Rhizoctonia solani Kühn (teleomorph: Thanatephorus cucumeris (Frank) Donk), is one of the most significant diseases of rice after blast, with reported yield losses ranging from 1.2% to as high as 69.0%. R. solani infects rice leaf sheaths at the base of culms, producing oblong, gray-brown, water-soaked lesions.

candidate_sources.title: Rice Sheath Blight Control | MU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: The first symptom is an oblong, water-soaked lesion on leaf sheaths at or near the water line. In two or three days the lesion will have a grayish-white center surrounded by a dark purplish- or reddish-brown margin. The disease is caused by the fungus Rhizoctonia solani, which survives in the soil as a sclerotium.

candidate_sources.title: Sheath blight - IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: Sheath blight is caused by the fungus Rhizoctonia solani. Early symptoms develop on the leaf sheaths near the water line as oval or ellipsoid greenish-gray water-soaked lesions; sclerotia form on infected tissues and survive in soil and plant debris. Yield losses of up to 50% have been reported under conducive environments.

candidate_sources.title: Tungro - IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: Tungro-infected plants show stunting, delayed flowering, reduced tiller numbers, small panicles, and yellow to orange leaf discoloration. Rice tungro disease results from coinfection by rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV) and rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV), transmitted by green leafhoppers (Nephotettix virescens). Yield losses can reach 100% when plants are infected at the seedling stage.

candidate_sources.title: RICE :: VIRAL DISEASES :: RICE TUNGRO DISEASE
candidate_sources.snippet: Rice tungro disease: leaves show yellow to orange discoloration and interveinal chlorosis, stunting, reduced tillering. Caused by Rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV) and Rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV), transmitted in a semipersistent manner by the green leafhopper Nephotettix virescens. Control through resistant varieties, roguing, and insecticide application.

candidate_sources.title: Rice Tungro Bacilliform Virus - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
candidate_sources.snippet: Rice tungro disease is caused by a complex of two viruses: rice tungro spherical virus (RTSV), which causes few symptoms and confers leafhopper transmissibility, and rice tungro bacilliform virus (RTBV), the major contributor to symptom production. Co-infection induces severe stunting and orange-yellow leaf discoloration; transmitted by green leafhopper Nephotettix virescens.

candidate_sources.title: A Brief Review on Present Status of Rice Tungro Disease: Types of Viruses, Vectors, Occurrence, Symptoms, Control and Resistant Rice Varieties
candidate_sources.snippet: A comprehensive review covering rice tungro disease virus types (RTBV, RTSV), green leafhopper vectors, geographic occurrence, symptomatology (stunting, orange-yellow discoloration), control measures, and resistant rice varieties.
